objects: a set of elements X = {x1, ..., xm}, not a fixed-length vector
assumptions: The function has to give the same answer no matter what order the set's elements are listed in (permutation invariance).
guarantees: Proves (not just claims) that a function is permutation invariant if and only if it can be written as: transform each element, add the results together, then transform the sum. This is a full if-and-only-if proof, not just an approximation result.
Also works out the matching rule for the equivariant version, where each element gets its own output.
formalism.operation: Run each set element through the same small network to get its own representation, add all those representations together, then run the sum through a second network to get the final output.

evidence_spans.objects: Now, if the input is a set X = {x1, . . . , xm}, then we would like the response of the function not to depend on the ordering of the elements in the set.
evidence_spans.assumptions: A function f acting on sets must be permutation invariant to the order of objects in the set, i.e. f({x1, ..., xm}) = f({xσ(1), ..., xσ(m)}) for any permutation σ.
evidence_spans.guarantees: A function S(X) operating on a set X can be a valid scoring function, i.e. it is permutation invariant to the elements in X, if and only if it can be decomposed in the form ρ(Σ_{x∈X} φ(x)), for suitable transformations φ and ρ.

notes: This is the only paper of the six with a full necessary-and-sufficient proof rather than just an approximation bound or empirical claim. Worth remembering for the recommendation step.
